title: Drinking After a Tattoo: How Long to Wait and Why It Matters
excerpt: How long to wait to drink after a tattoo, why alcohol before a session means more bleeding, why most artists refuse drunk clients, and how drinking affects aftercare.
metaDescription: How long to wait before drinking after a tattoo, why alcohol before a session means more bleeding, and how drinking affects healing and aftercare.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** wait at least 24 to 48 hours after getting a tattoo before you drink, and skip alcohol for at least 24 hours before your appointment too. A fresh tattoo is an open wound. Alcohol widens your blood vessels and can make your blood a little slower to clot, which tends to mean more bleeding and oozing at exactly the time your skin is trying to seal. After the first couple of days, a drink or two won't ruin your tattoo. What does the damage is heavy drinking during the two-week healing window, mostly because it leaves you dehydrated and makes aftercare mistakes far more likely.

**The quick rules:**

- **Before the tattoo:** no alcohol for at least 24 hours. Don't show up drunk or hungover. Most artists will refuse to tattoo you if you're intoxicated.
- **Right after:** no alcohol for at least 24 to 48 hours while the tattoo is still weeping fluid.
- **Weeks one and two:** light drinking only, with water alongside. Don't let a night out derail cleaning, moisturizing, or keeping the tattoo out of pools, hot tubs, and dirty environments.
- **Always:** follow your own artist's aftercare instructions. If they're stricter than this guide, go with theirs.

> **See a doctor if:** your tattoo shows signs of infection, such as redness or swelling that keeps spreading after the first two or three days, increasing pain instead of improving pain, warmth, pus or a bad smell, red streaks running away from the tattoo, or a fever or chills. Get urgent care for a fever with a spreading red area, or any sign of a severe allergic reaction. If you take a prescription blood thinner, aspirin for your heart, or have a bleeding disorder, talk to your doctor before getting a tattoo at all. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Why Alcohol and Fresh Tattoos Don't Mix

To understand the waiting period, it helps to know what a tattoo actually does to your skin. A tattoo machine pushes needles into the second layer of skin (the dermis) thousands of times a minute, depositing ink there. Your body treats this as a wound. In the first day or two, the tattooed area bleeds a little, then oozes clear-to-yellow fluid called plasma, mixed with excess ink. Over the next several days a thin layer of new skin forms, and the area peels and flakes. The surface usually looks healed in about two to four weeks, while the deeper layers keep settling for a couple of months.

Alcohol interferes with this process in a few ways.

### 1. It widens your blood vessels

Alcohol is a vasodilator, meaning it relaxes and opens up blood vessels, especially the small ones near the skin. That's why some people get a flushed face after a drink. More blood flow near the surface means more bleeding from freshly punctured skin, both during the session and in the hours afterward.

### 2. It has a mild blood-thinning effect

Alcohol doesn't thin your blood the way a prescription anticoagulant does, but it does have a measurable short-term effect on platelets, the small blood cells that clump together to plug a wound. Research on alcohol and clotting generally finds that drinking can make platelets a little less sticky for a while, and heavy drinking has a stronger effect than light drinking. We cover this in detail in our guide to [whether alcohol thins your blood](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-thin-your-blood).

For a tattoo, that small effect matters more than it would for a paper cut. A tattoo is a wide area of skin punctured thousands of times. Even a slight delay in clotting adds up across that whole area.

### 3. It dehydrates you

Alcohol makes your kidneys release more water than usual by suppressing a hormone called vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone). Healing skin needs water and good circulation to rebuild. A dehydrated body is not in the best position to repair a large patch of damaged skin, and dry, tight skin is more likely to crack around the scabs.

### 4. It can blunt your immune response

A fresh tattoo is a doorway for bacteria until the surface seals. Heavy drinking is known to temporarily weaken parts of the immune system, including the white blood cells that respond first to a wound. Lab and animal research on alcohol and wound healing has found that alcohol exposure can slow wound closure and weaken the early immune response at the wound site. Human data specific to tattoos doesn't really exist, but the general picture is consistent enough that artists and dermatologists recommend taking it easy. For more on this, see our overview of [alcohol and the immune system](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-immune-system-complete-health-impact-2025).

### 5. It makes you careless

This is the one that ruins the most tattoos, and it isn't about chemistry at all. After a few drinks, people forget to wash their tattoo, fall asleep on it without a clean layer between it and the sheets, scratch it, pick at scabs, lean against grimy bar surfaces, get drinks spilled on it, or decide a midnight hot tub sounds like a great idea. Each of those raises the chance of infection or patchy healing far more than the alcohol itself.

## Drinking Before a Tattoo: Why Most Artists Say No

A lot of people think a couple of drinks before a session will take the edge off the pain or the nerves. It's an understandable instinct, but it backfires, and most professional artists will refuse to work on you if you've been drinking.

### More bleeding means a harder job and a worse result

When skin bleeds heavily during a session, blood and plasma pool on the surface and wash ink back out. The artist has to wipe constantly, can see the stencil and line work less clearly, and may need to go over areas more than once. Going over the same skin repeatedly causes more trauma, which can mean more swelling, longer healing, and a higher chance of scarring. Excess bleeding is also linked by artists to patchy healing, where some areas lose ink and need a touch-up.

### It doesn't really help with pain

Alcohol can dull pain a little while you're drinking, but it also tends to make people restless, fidgety, and less able to hold still, which is the last thing you want when someone is drawing permanent lines on you. Many people also find the session feels worse, not better, as the drinks wear off partway through.

### Intoxicated people can't consent

A tattoo is permanent. Someone who is drunk can't give clear, informed consent to a permanent procedure, and reputable studios take that seriously. Many studios have a written policy against tattooing anyone who appears intoxicated, and health and licensing rules in many US states and other countries prohibit tattooing someone who is under the influence. If you show up drunk, expect to be sent home, and don't be surprised if you lose your deposit.

### Hangovers count too

Showing up hungover is better than showing up drunk, but it's still a bad idea. The morning after drinking you're usually dehydrated, your blood sugar may be low, and your pain sensitivity is often higher. People who arrive hungover are more likely to feel lightheaded, nauseous, or faint during the session, especially for long pieces or sensitive spots. Some leftover blood-thinning and vessel-widening effects may also still be in play if you drank heavily.

**What to do instead before your appointment:**

- Skip alcohol for at least 24 hours (48 hours if you can, especially for a big piece).
- Sleep well the night before.
- Eat a proper meal one to two hours before the session.
- Drink plenty of water the day before and the day of.
- Bring a snack and a sugary drink for long sessions in case you feel lightheaded.
- Ask your artist about pain relievers ahead of time (see the section below).

## How Long to Wait After a Tattoo Before Drinking

There is no single official rule, but tattoo artists and aftercare guides converge on a similar timeline. Here's a practical breakdown.

### The first 24 to 48 hours: no alcohol

This is the most important window. Your tattoo is still bleeding lightly and weeping plasma and ink. Blood vessels are working to close up, and the area is at its most vulnerable to bacteria. This is also when swelling peaks. Alcohol's vessel-widening effect can mean more oozing and more swelling, and if the tattoo weeps a lot, excess fluid can dry into thick scabs that pull ink out when they come off.

Use these first two days to rest, drink water, keep the tattoo clean, and follow your artist's wrap and washing instructions.

### Days 3 to 14: light drinking is generally fine

Once the oozing has stopped and the tattoo has started to close, a drink or two is unlikely to harm it. This is the stage where the tattoo usually forms a thin, flaky layer and starts to itch and peel. Your goals here are to keep the skin clean, keep it moisturized with whatever your artist recommends, keep it out of water you can't control, and avoid picking or scratching.

If you drink during this period:

- Keep it moderate. A couple of drinks, not a big night.
- Drink a glass of water with each alcoholic drink.
- Wash and moisturize the tattoo before bed, no matter how late it is.
- Wear loose, clean clothing over it if you're going somewhere crowded or dirty.
- Don't fall asleep on fresh sheets you haven't washed recently, and avoid sleeping directly on the tattoo if you can.

### Weeks 2 to 4 and beyond: back to normal, with care

By two to four weeks, most tattoos look healed on the surface. The deeper skin is still settling, but normal moderate drinking is unlikely to cause problems. Keep protecting it from sun, since UV exposure is one of the main causes of long-term fading, and keep moisturizing if it's still dry.

**Larger pieces take longer.** A small wrist tattoo and a full back piece are not the same wound. If your tattoo covers a big area, took several hours, or was done in multiple long sessions, give it more time before drinking and be more cautious through the healing weeks. Big tattoos put more stress on your body overall, and some people feel tired or slightly unwell for a day or two after a long session.

## The Aftercare Interplay: Where Drinking Actually Causes Problems

Most of the real risk from drinking with a new tattoo comes from what drinking leads you to do. Here are the common situations and how to handle them.

### Parties and bars

Bars, clubs, and house parties are crowded, sweaty, and not especially clean. A fresh tattoo can get bumped, rubbed against strangers, splashed with drinks, or touched by people who want a closer look. If you go out in the first week or two:

- Cover the tattoo with loose, clean clothing, or follow your artist's advice on a breathable protective film if they use one.
- Don't let people touch it.
- Wash your hands before touching it yourself.
- Avoid leaning it against tables, bar tops, or walls.

### Pools, hot tubs, lakes, and the ocean

Soaking a fresh tattoo is one of the most common aftercare mistakes, and it often happens at parties and on vacations when people are drinking. Standing water, including hot tubs, pools, lakes, and the sea, can carry bacteria, and soaking softens scabs so they lift and take ink with them. Most artists say no soaking for at least two weeks, or until the tattoo has fully peeled. Showers are fine; baths and swimming are not.

### Falling asleep without aftercare

After a night of drinking, it's easy to skip washing and moisturizing and just go to bed. A tattoo that hasn't been cleaned can collect bacteria overnight, and a weeping tattoo can stick to sheets. Pulling the sheet off in the morning can rip away healing skin and ink. If you know you'll be out late, clean and moisturize the tattoo before you leave, and put clean sheets on your bed.

### Scratching and picking

Healing tattoos itch, and alcohol can make itchy skin feel worse for some people because of the flushing and dryness it causes. (We look at why in our article on [itchy skin after drinking](/never-hungover/itchy-skin-after-drinking).) Scratching or picking at flakes and scabs is a quick way to pull out ink and introduce bacteria. Pat or lightly slap the area instead, and keep it moisturized.

### Sun exposure

Day drinking outdoors in the first few weeks is a double hit: alcohol dehydrates you and the sun damages healing skin and fades ink. Keep a new tattoo covered with clothing in the sun until it's fully healed. Most artists say to hold off on sunscreen until the surface has completely healed, then use it every time afterward.

## Pain Relievers, Alcohol, and Tattoos

People often reach for pain relievers before or after a tattoo, and sometimes combine them with alcohol. A few things to know:

- **Aspirin and NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen):** these affect platelets and can increase bleeding, so many artists ask clients to avoid them for about 24 hours before a session. Alcohol plus these medicines also raises the risk of stomach irritation and bleeding. Our guides on [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) and [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) go deeper.
- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol):** it doesn't affect clotting, so some artists prefer it if you need something for pain. It has its own issue with alcohol, though: it's processed by the liver, and combining it with heavy drinking raises the risk of liver damage. See our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).
- **Numbing creams:** some artists allow topical numbing products and some don't, because certain products can change how skin takes ink. Ask before you buy one.
- **Prescription blood thinners and daily aspirin:** if a doctor has you on warfarin, a newer anticoagulant, clopidogrel, or daily aspirin for your heart, **do not stop it to get a tattoo.** Talk to your doctor first about whether a tattoo is a good idea and how to plan for it. Alcohol can also interact with some of these medicines, which we cover in our guide to [blood thinners and alcohol](/never-hungover/blood-thinners-and-alcohol).

## Signs Your Tattoo Isn't Healing Well

Some redness, swelling, tenderness, and oozing in the first two or three days is normal. So is itching, flaking, and a cloudy or dull look in the first couple of weeks. These signs are not normal and deserve attention:

- Redness or swelling that is **spreading** or getting worse after day three
- Pain that is **increasing** rather than easing
- Skin that feels hot to the touch
- Pus, green or yellow discharge, or a bad smell
- Red streaks spreading away from the tattoo
- Fever, chills, or feeling generally unwell
- Raised, bumpy, intensely itchy areas, especially only in one ink color, which can be a sign of an allergic reaction to the pigment
- Blistering or open sores that don't seem to be closing

If you notice signs of infection, see a doctor rather than trying to treat it yourself. Infections caught early are usually easy to treat, but they can get serious if ignored. And if a doctor prescribes antibiotics, check whether you need to avoid alcohol with them; our guide to [antibiotics and alcohol](/never-hungover/antibiotics-and-alcohol) explains which ones matter most.

## Who Should Be Extra Careful

The basic waiting period works for most healthy adults. Take more care, and ideally talk to a doctor before your appointment, if you:

- Take a blood thinner, daily aspirin, or other medicine that affects bleeding
- Have a bleeding or clotting disorder
- Have diabetes or another condition that affects wound healing or circulation
- Have a weakened immune system, from illness or medication
- Have a history of keloids or raised scars
- Drink heavily on a regular basis, since long-term heavy drinking can affect clotting, liver function, and healing more than an occasional drink does
- Have a skin condition such as eczema or psoriasis in the area being tattooed

If cutting back on drinking for a few days around a tattoo feels genuinely hard, that's worth noticing and possibly worth talking to a doctor about. That's beyond the scope of this guide, but it's a fair signal to pay attention to.

## How to Have a Drink Without Wrecking Your Healing

If you've waited the first couple of days and want to enjoy a drink while your tattoo heals, these habits keep the risk low:

1. **Drink less than usual.** Healing is a good reason to keep it to one or two.
2. **Hydrate on purpose.** Alternate every drink with a glass of water, and drink more water the next morning. Our guide to [rehydrating after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) covers what works.
3. **Eat first.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream.
4. **Do your aftercare before you go out.** Clean, moisturize, and dress the tattoo in clean, loose clothing so you're covered even if you get home late.
5. **Stay dry.** No hot tubs, pools, or ocean swims until your artist says it's healed.
6. **Sleep smart.** Fresh sheets, and try not to lie directly on the tattoo.
7. **Skip the next-day sun.** If you're hungover, you're already dehydrated. Don't add sun exposure on healing skin.

### Where hangover supplements fit (and where they don't)

Some people take hangover supplements when they drink. To be clear: **no supplement speeds up tattoo healing, and none makes it OK to drink in the first 24 to 48 hours.** There's no good evidence that DHM or any other hangover product affects how a tattoo heals.

What DHM (dihydromyricetin) is studied for is how the body handles alcohol and hangover symptoms. Most of that research is in animals and lab settings, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. If you already use it on nights you drink, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when. The habits that actually help most are the boring ones in our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover): drink less, drink slower, eat, and hydrate.

## The Bottom Line

- **Before a tattoo:** no alcohol for at least 24 hours. Don't show up drunk or hungover. Reputable artists won't tattoo someone who is intoxicated.
- **After a tattoo:** wait at least 24 to 48 hours before drinking, while the tattoo is still bleeding and weeping.
- **During healing (about two to four weeks):** light drinking is generally fine. Heavy drinking can slow healing and makes aftercare mistakes much more likely.
- **The biggest risks are behavioral:** skipped cleaning, soaking in pools and hot tubs, scratching, dirty environments, and sun.
- **See a doctor** for spreading redness, increasing pain, pus, red streaks, or fever.
- **Your artist's instructions come first.** They know your skin, your piece, and the products they used.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How long after a tattoo can I drink alcohol?**

Most tattoo artists recommend waiting at least 24 to 48 hours after your session before drinking. That covers the window when the tattoo is still an open wound that oozes blood, plasma, and ink. After that, a drink or two is unlikely to ruin a tattoo, but heavy drinking during the first two weeks of healing can slow recovery and make aftercare mistakes more likely. Follow your artist's specific instructions if they differ.

**Can I drink the night before getting a tattoo?**

It's best not to. Most artists ask you to avoid alcohol for at least 24 hours before your appointment. Alcohol widens blood vessels and can make your blood slightly slower to clot, which tends to mean more bleeding during the session. Showing up hungover also makes you dehydrated, more sensitive to pain, and more likely to feel faint or nauseous in the chair.

**Will a tattoo artist tattoo you if you're drunk?**

Reputable artists will not. Someone who is intoxicated can't give clear consent, tends to bleed more, and often can't sit still. Many studios have a written policy against tattooing anyone who appears drunk or high, and health regulations in many US states and other countries prohibit it. If you turn up drunk, expect to be turned away and possibly to lose your deposit.

**Does alcohol make a tattoo bleed more?**

It can. Alcohol widens small blood vessels near the skin and has a mild effect on platelets, the blood cells that help form clots. The effect from a drink or two is small, but heavier drinking before or during a session is commonly linked by artists to more bleeding and oozing. Extra bleeding can push ink back out of the skin and make the line work harder to see while the artist works.

**Can drinking alcohol ruin a new tattoo?**

One or two drinks a couple of days after your session is unlikely to ruin it. The bigger risks are indirect: heavy drinking that leaves you dehydrated and run-down while your skin is healing, and drunk mistakes like sleeping on the tattoo without cleaning it, picking at scabs, jumping in a hot tub or pool, or getting a spilled drink or dirt on an open wound. Those are what cause infections, patchy healing, and faded spots.

**Can I take ibuprofen or aspirin before a tattoo?**

Many artists ask you to avoid aspirin and other NSAIDs like ibuprofen for about 24 hours before a session, because they can affect clotting and increase bleeding. If you take aspirin or any blood thinner because a doctor prescribed it, don't stop it on your own; talk to your doctor before booking the tattoo. Combining these pain relievers with alcohol also raises the risk of stomach irritation and bleeding.

**Is it OK to drink at a party a week after getting a tattoo?**

Usually, yes, in moderation. By a week in, the surface is closing and peeling. Keep it to a few drinks, drink water alongside, keep the tattoo covered with clean, loose clothing in crowded places, stay out of pools and hot tubs, and wash and moisturize it before bed as usual. Avoid getting drunk enough that you forget your aftercare.

**Does DHM help a tattoo heal?**

No. There's no good evidence that DHM or any hangover supplement affects how a tattoo heals. DHM is studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms, mostly in animal and lab research with limited human data. Good aftercare, rest, hydration, and going easy on alcohol are what matter for healing.
